name: PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Charoen Pokphand Indonesia — the protein cycle has turned; the multiple has not
frontmatter.summary: CPIN's nine-month result is an actual, not a hope: sales and attributable profit both rose sharply on a wider margin as the corn price it paid ran below the forward curve. The shares have de-rated to a fraction of their year-high against those earnings. Our target is Rp3,650, a total return of 63.3%; the discounted cash flow alone does not get there, and we say so.
thesis: The nine-month 2026 result is reported, not forecast — sales of IDR60,200bn against IDR50,600bn and attributable profit of IDR5,180bn — and the fourth quarter only has to hold the run-rate for the full year to beat the last audited one.

The margin widened because the input cost fell, not because prices were pushed: cost of goods sold of IDR49,600bn grew slower than sales while the corn CPIN bought ran below the deck's forward curve [S2, S0]. The national SPHP feed-corn programme is small and aimed at layer smallholders, not the cause [S8].

The group is the scale leader in a domestic protein market it serves end to end — feed, day-old chicks, broiler growing and processed chicken — and nine-tenths of sales are domestic, so the rupiah and the global feed complex reach it as costs, not as demand [S2].
The shares trade at 6.9x trailing earnings and 1.1x book against a year-high of Rp4,810, so the de-rating, not the earnings, is the opportunity [S0].

The discounted cash flow is the discipline and it is the bear in this report: at a cost of capital of 11.9% and a working-capital intensity that eats most of the incremental sales, it values the equity well below the price. The target leans on the earnings cross-checks, and the valuation section states the tension rather than hiding it.

catalysts.event: Nine-month public expose and any fourth-quarter guidance on margins and corn cost
FY2026 audited statements — the first full year to carry the recovered margin
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration

blocks.text: We initiate on CPIN at BUY with a target of Rp3,650, a total return of 63.3% from a price of Rp2,370 [S0]. The variant view is not that the poultry cycle is recovering — the nine-month statements already say it is — but that the market has stopped paying for the recovery at all. The shares sit at their year-low, Rp2,370 against a year-high of Rp4,810, on 6.9x trailing earnings and 1.1x book, while the company has just reported attributable profit of IDR5,180bn for nine months against IDR50,600bn of sales in the comparable period [S0, S2].

The recovery is a cost story before it is a price story. Nine-month sales of IDR60,200bn were well ahead of the prior year, but cost of goods sold of IDR49,600bn grew more slowly, and the margin that came out of that gap is what lifted profit before tax to IDR6,680bn [S2]. The input relief is the corn price: CPIN's 2026 cost of goods sold grew slower than sales while the corn it bought ran below the deck's forward curve [S2, F10, S0]. The national SPHP feed-corn programme is a small, dated support for layer smallholders, not the mechanism behind an integrated producer's margin [S8, F31]; it is a risk to monitor, not the thing an investor is underwriting.

The forward arithmetic is the strongest part of the bull case, and it is worth stating plainly. Nine-month basic earnings per share were Rp316 [S2, F13], so the run-rate leaves the shares at Rp2,370 on single-digit forward earnings, with a forward dividend yield of 9.3% on our Rp221 distribution and a payout the board has just raised to 52.3% [S5, S7]. That is an income floor the price is not paying for, and it is why the earnings frame carries weight even though the cash-flow frame does not.

What moves the value, in order: the gross margin, which carries the corn and soymeal complex through a partial pass-through to feed and chicken prices; the working-capital intensity, because inventory and receivables absorb most of each additional rupiah of sales and that is what holds the discounted cash flow down; and the multiple the market is willing to pay for a business whose earnings have just grown by half. The first two are modelled; the third is what the cross-checks measure, and it is where the target comes from.

We are explicit about the shape of the answer. The discounted cash flow, our primary method, values the shares at Rp1,636 — below the market price. The earnings methods value them at Rp5,035 and Rp5,058. The weighted answer is Rp3,340, and the target adds the dividend we expect over the next twelve months. A reader who believes the cash-flow frame should not own this at the current price; a reader who believes the earnings frame should. The valuation section sets out which we think is right and why.

CPIN is the largest poultry and animal-feed group in Indonesia, and it is vertically integrated from the feed mill to the plate. The nine-month segment disclosure shows the shape of it: broiler growing contributed IDR26,980bn of sales, animal feed IDR20,740bn, processed chicken IDR8,150bn, day-old chicks IDR3,440bn and other activities IDR892bn [S2]. The same ordering held for the last full year, when broiler contributed IDR34,000bn, feed IDR21,000bn and day-old chicks IDR3,500bn of a IDR70,700bn top line [S5]. The mix matters for the thesis: the group sells the feed, the chick and the grown bird, so a fall in the feed input cost reaches it twice — once as a margin on feed sold to third-party farmers and once as a lower cost of production in its own broiler and processed-chicken operations.

The business is domestic. Nine-month sales inside Indonesia were IDR59,940bn against exports of IDR256bn [S2]. That is close to a pure rupiah revenue base, and it means the group's exposure to the currency and to the global feed complex runs through the cost line rather than the demand line — imported soymeal and imported feed additives are priced in dollars, while the chicken and the feed are sold in rupiah.

The group is controlled from Thailand. The Jiaravanon family holds 55.5% directly through Charoen Pokphand Indonesia Group, public investors hold 38.5% and UBS AG Singapore holds 6.0% [S5]. The two registers do not agree and we treat that as a data gap rather than smoothing it: the press register (group 55.5%, public 38.5%, UBS 6.0%) [S5] and the pack register (free float 15.4%, insiders 71.5%) [S0] differ by a wide double-digit margin on the public float and a narrower one on insiders; the difference is consistent with a large part of the "public" register being nominee or affiliated money the pack classes as insider, but we cannot prove it from the sources we hold. On the pack's number the free float is a small fraction of IDR38,863.3bn of market value, and on the press number a larger one; we use the pack for the liquidity test because it is the more conservative.

The strategy is capacity and integration rather than new geography. In August 2025 the group, through its ninety-nine per cent-owned PT Charoen Pokphand Jaya Farm, completed the purchase of poultry breeding facilities in East Java and North Sulawesi from PT Satwa Utama Raya for IDR431bn [S6]. The seller is itself a ninety-nine per cent-controlled affiliate, so the transaction is a related-party one and is treated as such under governance. The direction is consistent with the segment mix: breeding capacity feeds the day-old-chick and broiler businesses that together are the majority of sales.

Indonesian poultry is a short-cycle protein business. A broiler reaches slaughter weight in weeks, so
supply responds to price faster than in most agricultural industries, and the cycle is driven by
feed cost and by the live-bird price rather than by long-lived assets. Feed is the largest single
cost in the chain, and corn is the largest single input in feed, which is why the corn policy of the
government of the day is the most important variable in the sector. The industry is also unusually
policy-visible: the school-meals programme has made chicken and eggs a matter of public procurement,
and the government has taken an active interest in both the price farmers receive and the price
consumers pay.

The industry's economics are set by two prices the company does not control: the cost of feed grain and the live-bird price. The nine-month result is a clean illustration of what happens when the first falls faster than the second — sales of IDR60,200bn against cost of goods sold of IDR49,600bn, with profit before tax of IDR6,680bn [S2]. The segment split supports that reading: the feed segment is a third of sales and the broiler segment nearly half, so a feed-cost move is felt on both sides of the book [S2].

The policy items are supporting, not causal. The national food agency scheduled the release of 242 kt of feed corn from March 2026 under its SPHP programme, aimed at the volatility in corn prices that hits poultry producers' production costs [S8]. That volume is for small and medium layer (egg) farmers, and at 242 kt it is a small fraction of an industry whose listed leader alone sells IDR20,740bn of feed in nine months [S2, F4]; it is not the reason a feed-to-plate group's margin recovered, and we do not treat it as one. In November 2026 the agriculture ministry set out a supply-chain scheme linking corn farmers, cooperatives, breeders and the state logistics agency, with surplus corn bought into warehouse receipts and released in the lean season [S9]. Both are dated, reversible supports to the corn price — worth monitoring, not worth underwriting. The margin itself comes from the corn price CPIN paid running below the deck's forward curve, which is visible in the cost line: cost of goods sold grew slower than sales [S2, F10, S0].

Demand has a policy leg of its own, but we do not put a number on it. The free nutritious meals programme has put chicken and eggs into institutional menus, and the poultry producers that supply slaughterhouses and processors stand to gain volume if the programme's kitchen network keeps expanding [S3]. The same reporting notes that increased production to serve those kitchens would also pull through demand for day-old chicks and feed — the two segments where CPIN's integration gives it the most leverage [S3]. No source we hold gives the programme's kitchen count, beneficiary number or protein content, so we carry no institutional volume in the base case and none in the bull; it is a qualitative support in the bull narrative, not a quantified driver, and it is listed as a signpost rather than as a dated catalyst with a value attached.

Competitive position. CPIN is the largest listed poultry producer by revenue in the sector, ahead of its nearest listed peer, and it is the only one of the large players that combines a feed business of national scale with broiler growing, breeding and processing under one roof [S3]. The moat is distribution density and integration rather than brand: feed is a commodity sold on price and availability, and the advantage belongs to the producer with the mills, the breeding farms and the cold chain in the same place. That is a real but bounded moat — it protects the cost position, not the selling price, and it does not stop the live-bird price from falling when the industry over-supplies.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and concentrated in the corn and soymeal complex, which is why the policy intervention matters so much. Buyer power is moderate: feed customers are fragmented farmers, but the live-bird price is set in a spot market where the group is a price taker. New entrants face capital and biosecurity barriers but not regulatory ones. Substitutes are weak within protein and strong across it, since fish and eggs compete for the same household budget. Rivalry is intense and cyclical, and the listed peer set shows it — in the same nine months one large peer grew profit while a smaller one swung to a loss [S3].

The structural question for Indonesian poultry is whether the industry can consolidate enough to
stop the boom-bust cycle in live-bird prices. Integration helps the integrated producer but does not
solve the industry's coordination problem, because the marginal supply still comes from independent
farmers who respond to last season's price. That is why the sector's margins have historically
mean-reverted, and why we treat the current margin as a level to be held rather than a level to be
extrapolated.

History. The last four audited years show a business that grew its top line steadily and its profit in a cycle. Revenue went from IDR56,868bn to IDR70,700bn, but operating profit fell in the middle of that run before recovering to IDR8,133bn in the last audited year [S0]. The recovery continued into the current year: nine-month sales of IDR60,200bn and attributable profit of IDR5,180bn [S2], with basic earnings per share of Rp316 for the nine months [S2].

Our forecast. FY2026E revenue of IDR84,133bn carries the nine-month actual and runs the fourth quarter at the witnessed growth rate; the growth rate then steps down to 7.0% and tapers towards the house macro deck's long-run rate for Indonesia, because nine-tenths of sales are domestic and no source discloses the new capacity that would repeat a twenty per cent year [S0, S2]. FY2026E EBITDA is IDR10,173bn at a margin of 12.1%, essentially the last audited year's 11.9% — the calibration the method card asks for, and the reason we set the gross-margin input the way we did. From FY2027E the house agricultural deck's corn and soymeal curves, which sit above spot, are charged through the two cost links at a sixty per cent pass-through, and that is what compresses the margin in the outer years [S0].

Margins and costs. The gross margin is the whole story of this name. The witnessed nine-month rate is the anchor; the deck's forward corn and soymeal prices are the risk. The input we set is the margin before the deck's cost links; the realised margin the model produces is 17.7% in FY2026E, 15.2% in FY2027E and 14.8% in FY2028E. That is the path a reader should hold us to: FY2026E reproduces the witnessed rate because its first nine months are an actual, and from FY2027E the deck's corn and soymeal curves, which sit above the spot price CPIN paid in 2026, take about two and a half points out of the margin [S0, S2]. We carry a corn exposure of 19.0% of cost of goods sold and a soymeal exposure of 9.0%, both estimates ordered from the disclosed segment mix rather than published input bills, and we say so plainly: the company does not disclose its raw-material bill, and the red team should read those two numbers as magnitudes, not measurements [S2, S8]. Overhead is held at the last audited year's ratio of 6.1% of sales, flat in real terms [S0].

Cash flow, capex and working capital. This is where the model and the market part company. Operating cash flow exceeded net profit in the last audited year, which is the right sign, but the balance sheet is working-capital heavy: inventory and receivables together are a large multiple of payables, and operating working capital runs at roughly a fifth of revenue [S0]. At the growth rate we forecast, that absorbs most of each incremental rupiah of sales, and it is the main reason the discounted cash flow in the valuation section comes out where it does. Capex is held at the last audited year's ratio of 2.5% of sales [S0]; the breeding-facility purchase of IDR431bn sits in investing cash flow as an acquisition and is not grossed up into the capex line [S6].

Balance sheet. Net debt was IDR2,201bn at the last audited year-end, or 0.3 times EBITDA [S0]. The valuation, however, deducts the data pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet, where net debt is more than double that figure and net debt/EBITDA is about half a turn rather than a third [S0]. The nine-month statements show total assets of IDR53,260bn, liabilities of IDR16,880bn and equity of IDR36,380bn [S2]. The same June balance sheet shows operating working capital up by roughly a sixth in six months against nine-month revenue growth of about an eighth annualised [S0, S2] — the working-capital build the cash-flow section warns about is already happening faster than sales, and it is in the bear case rather than left as a forward risk. The group is not levered against the earnings it is now producing, and the interest cover implied by profit before tax of IDR6,680bn is comfortable [S2]. Return on equity was 17.5% in the last audited year and we forecast 19.2% for the current one [S0].

Capital allocation. The dividend is the clearest signal the board sends. For the 2025 financial year the company declared Rp180 a share, IDR2,950bn in total, a payout of 52.3% of attributable profit, up from the prior year's ratio [S5, S7]. That is a shareholder-return policy rather than a token, and we hold the ratio flat in the forecast.

Earnings-quality flags. Three things we watch, and one we cannot check. First, receivables grew several times faster than revenue in the last audited year, and inventory grew faster than cost of goods sold — both are divergence flags under the house screen, and both are consistent with a business extending credit to farmers and holding grain, but they need to be watched rather than assumed benign [S0]. Second, the profit improvement is a margin effect rather than a revenue effect, which is the higher-quality kind, but it is policy-dependent and therefore reversible [S2, S8]. Third, the group's growth in assets in the current year has run well ahead of its growth in equity, which is what a working-capital build looks like and is the reason we do not treat the reported profit as free cash [S2]. The accruals ratio is clean: FY2025 attributable profit of IDR5,640bn was covered by operating cash flow, so earnings are not outrunning cash [S0, S7]. The one line we cannot verify is depreciation: the data pack carries a charge that is small relative to a fixed-asset base of this size, and the company's own statements were not reachable for this revision, so the D&A line remains the pack's and is likely understated [S0]. We flag it as an open data gap rather than model around it, and the direction of the error is one-way and against the call. Depreciation does not touch EBITDA, and the multiple legs are struck on the reported FY2025A EPS and reported FY2025A EBITDA [S5, S7, S0], which a forecast depreciation rate does not enter, so the low line neither flatters those legs nor carries them. Its measurable effect is inside the forecast: depreciation of 0.5% of revenue against capital spending of 2.5% of revenue understates the cash tax shield every year of the projection, so the discounted cash flow — already the leg that values the shares below the price — is if anything too low rather than too high. The target is accordingly not raised on the multiple legs while this line is unsourced, and the DCF understates rather than overstates value.

Why this method set. POULTRY_FEED is valued on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with earnings and EBITDA multiples as cross-checks, because the business is a going concern whose value comes from the cash it converts over a cycle rather than from a finite reserve or a contracted revenue stream [S0]. The method card's discipline applies: growth has to be paid for by reinvestment, the discount rate is pinned to the house band, and the terminal value has to survive a multiple test.

The cost of capital. The build is the house one: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the industry default, levered to 1.08 at the group's own debt-to-equity of 0.25, giving a cost of equity of 13.0% and a WACC of 11.9% [S0]. The cost of equity is at the top of the house band for a rupiah reporter — a few basis points above it, not inside it — and we accept it there because the balance-of-payments regime the macro desk has flagged is a rupiah risk this name carries through imported soymeal, not a reason to cut the discount rate [S0].

The primary method. The discounted cash flow values the equity at Rp1,636, with the terminal value at 39.9% of the total — a low share, which is the right shape for a business whose near-term cash conversion is the question [S0]. The drag is working capital: at a fifth of revenue and with sales growing, the incremental investment in inventory and receivables is larger than capex in every forecast year, and that is what turns an EBITDA of IDR10,173bn into a much smaller free cash flow. We have not softened that assumption, because it is what the last four years of balance sheets show [S0].

The cross-checks, and the divergence. The earnings methods value the shares far above the cash-flow method. The P/E cross-check gives Rp5,035 on 14.6 times FY2025A earnings and the EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp5,058 on 10.4 times FY2025A EBITDA, respectively 207.8% and 209.2% above the primary [S0]. Both legs are deliberately struck on the last audited year, not on FY2026E: applying our own forecast to a historical multiple would put our estimate on both sides of the cross-check, and FY2025A is the last year the market could see in full when it set the price. The horizon difference is real and we state it: on FY2026E EPS the same P/E multiple would give a materially higher number, so the published gap is a lower bound on the divergence, not an upper one. That is a very wide gap and it must be explained rather than averaged away. The explanation is that the two frames are answering different questions. The multiple frame asks what the market has historically paid for this earnings stream and what its peers pay; on 6.9x trailing earnings the answer is that the market is paying very little. The cash-flow frame asks what the business can distribute after funding its own growth; on a working-capital-heavy, capital-consuming growth path the answer is much less. Both are true. The weighted answer of Rp3,340 gives the cash-flow frame half the weight, which is the house convention for this industry, and the target of Rp3,650 adds the dividend we expect over the next twelve months.

The implicit re-rating, stated plainly. The two earnings legs carry half the weight and both apply a multiple above the one the market pays today. The P/E leg's 14.6 on FY2025A earnings is a re-rating to roughly twice the 6.9x trailing multiple at the current price [S0]. That multiple is the mechanical average of two very different populations: the listed poultry peers, which trade on low single-digit P/E and EBITDA multiples because the market treats their earnings as trough-cycle, and CPIN's own five-year mean in the mid-twenties, which the market paid when the group was compounding capacity through a growth phase. Peer-anchored, the legs would not exceed the current price and this call would not exist; own-history-anchored, it implies a re-rating above today's multiple. We choose the average because the truth is in between: the market is pricing trough earnings and a trough multiple at the same time, and the recovery we are underwriting is the one that restores the historical multiple as the cycle earnings normalise, not a multiple above the historical mean. A reader who thinks the low-single-digit peer multiple is the correct perpetual level for this earnings stream should not own the shares, and that is the single assumption the BUY rests on.

The terminal-value test. The DCF's terminal value is 39.9% of the total, and it implies an exit EV/EBITDA far below the 10.4 times the cross-check pays and below the multiple the market pays for the business today [S0]. That is the mandatory multiple-survival test, and it fails in the conservative direction: a perpetuity that values the terminal business at a fraction of the cross-check multiple is either saying the cross-check is too high — which is our view, given the industry's mean-reverting margins — or that the terminal margin is set too low. We take it as the first and we do not raise the exit multiple to rescue the DCF; the tension is stated, not smoothed.

What today's price implies. The reverse calculation does not bracket: at a price of Rp2,370 the discounted cash flow cannot be made to reach the market price by varying the growth input within any plausible range, which is another way of saying the market is not valuing this business on distributable cash flow at all [S0]. Because the DCF value sits below the price, closing the gap requires a HIGHER perpetual growth rate than we assume or a LOWER cost of capital than the house band allows — the arithmetic runs that way, and neither is available to us: growth above nominal GDP is not a perpetuity a cyclical feed business earns, and a cost of capital below the band is a rupiah risk we are not prepared to underwrite. We think the more likely reading is that the market is pricing the cycle rather than the company: the shares have fallen from Rp4,810 to Rp2,370 while earnings rose, and a market that expects the margin to mean-revert will not pay a cash-flow multiple for it.

The sensitivity grid is driven by the gross margin and the cost of capital, because those are the two inputs that carry most of the value: the margin is where the corn price lands, and the cost of capital is where the country risk lands. A reader who wants a different answer should move those two, not the terminal growth rate. In the published WACC/terminal-growth grid, each row is a terminal growth step and each column a WACC step: the value falls as the WACC rises across a row and rises with terminal growth down a column. We checked one cell against a hand DCF and the signs are right; the axis labels have been re-read against the engine's array order so a reader cannot reverse them.

The bear case, with likelihood and impact. The highest-likelihood downside is the reversal of the input-cost relief: corn returns to the deck's forward curve, which sits well above the spot price CPIN paid in 2026, and the house agricultural deck already prices corn and soymeal above spot [S0]. If the deck's curve is right, the margin gives back the step it took, and because the group passes only part of a cost move through to feed and chicken prices, the profit effect is larger than the cost effect. The national SPHP feed-corn programme is too small to offset that — 242 kt for layer smallholders is not a lever on an integrated producer's cost base [S8, F31] — so we do not count on it. The second is demand: the free-meals programme is the main incremental demand driver named in the press, and a programme that is reshuffled or slowed takes the volume leg with it [S3]; beyond the programme, a source we already trust opens by projecting CPIN's revenue weaker on softening household purchasing power [S6], which is a demand-side downside the earlier draft missed. The third is price realisation: the live-bird and DOC prices are set daily in a spot market the group does not clear, and the peer set shows how fast that can turn — one listed peer swung to a loss and another is still loss-making on strong revenue growth [S3]. The bear therefore cuts the margin by three points, carrying both the cost leg and a price fall, mirrored exactly by the bull; it is not a volume-only shock. The fourth is currency: soymeal is imported and the rupiah is under balance-of-payments pressure in the house macro view, so the protein input costs more in rupiah at an unchanged dollar price [S0]. The fifth is operational and biological — disease and biosecurity — for which we have no source in this draft and which we therefore flag as unquantified rather than pretend to model.

Governance and structure risks are covered under governance, and the honest summary of that section is that the related-party flow table, the auditor and any pledge are not assessed. Liquidity is not the constraint the earlier draft said it was: the pack's free float is 15.4% of a IDR38,863.3bn market value, and three-month average daily turnover is IDR96.2bn [S0], a low single-digit percentage of the pack's free float a day and adequate depth for institutional positions. The engine charges no liquidity discount, and on that turnover we accept it; on the press register's larger float the ratio would be lower still, so the conclusion does not depend on which register is right.

The scenarios are mirrored. The bear cuts the growth rate and the gross margin; the bull adds the same amounts to the same two drivers, and nothing else. Probabilities are 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull. The bear values the shares at Rp2,823, the base at Rp3,554 and the bull at Rp4,668 [S0]. Note that even the bear is above the current price: that is a statement about how far the shares have fallen, not a claim that the downside is small — the bear's own cash-flow value is below the price, and the scenario values inherit the same multiple-heavy blend as the base.

Signposts that would change our view, in both directions. For the better: corn staying near the spot price CPIN paid rather than returning to the deck's forward curve [S0]; a second consecutive quarter of margin at the witnessed level; evidence that the free-meals programme is converting into contracted volume for the group's processing business [S3]. For the worse: corn returning to the deck's curve while live-bird prices stay flat; a working-capital build that outruns sales; any related-party transaction larger than the breeding-facility purchase already disclosed [S6].

Ownership and control. The company is controlled by the Jiaravanon family through Charoen Pokphand Indonesia Group at 55.5%, with public investors at 38.5% and UBS AG Singapore at 6.0% [S5]. The pack's register — free float 15.4%, insiders 71.5% [S0] — is not consistent with that structure and we say so rather than asserting it: the two differ by a wide double-digit margin on the public float and a narrower one on insiders, and we have not sourced who the difference is. We use the pack's lower float for the liquidity test. Control is concentrated and stable, which is the norm for the large IDX consumer names; on the evidence we hold the governance conclusion is "not assessed" rather than a rating, because the related-party flow table and the auditor are missing.

Related parties. The group buys from and sells to affiliated companies, and the transaction we can source is the August 2025 purchase of poultry breeding facilities from PT Satwa Utama Raya for IDR431bn, a company ninety-nine per cent controlled by CPIN itself, executed through a ninety-nine per cent-owned subsidiary [S6]. That is an internal reorganisation rather than a value transfer out of the group, and the consideration was disclosed to the exchange. We have not been able to source a full related-party flow table for this revision — no purchases/sales percentage of revenue or COGS — and under the house screen that is a pre-thesis gate, so we do not assert that the flows are small. The household screen is run where the data exists: accruals are clean (the Sloan ratio is negligible, as the financial section shows) and we found no pledge, no special-notation letter and no auditor change in the sources we hold, but the absence of a search result is not a clean bill, and it is recorded as a gap.

Dividend record. The company pays a substantial and rising dividend: Rp180 a share for the 2025 financial year, IDR2,950bn in total, a payout of 52.3% of attributable profit [S5, S7]. The payment was made in June 2026 [S7]. A controlling shareholder that takes cash out through dividends rather than through related-party balances is the better version of concentrated ownership, and the record supports that reading.

Board and auditor. The board is led by a president director who has spoken publicly for the company on its acquisition disclosures [S6]. We have not been able to source the audit opinion or the auditor identity for this draft, because the company's own statements were not reachable; that is a gap in this section and it is reported as one, not filled with an assumption.

ESG exposures. The material ones are biosecurity and animal welfare in the growing operations, antibiotic use in feed, and the labour intensity of processing. The company's own sustainability reporting was not reachable for this draft. On the social side, the free-meals programme makes the group's product part of a public nutrition policy, which is a reputational exposure as much as a demand opportunity [S3].

The dated catalysts are the nine-month public expose and any fourth-quarter guidance, the FY2026 audited statements, and the FY2026 dividend declaration at the annual meeting [S2, S7]. The first is the nearest and the most informative: the company has reported nine months of a recovered margin and the market will want to know whether the fourth quarter holds it.

Between updates we watch four things. The gross margin, quarter by quarter, because it is the whole thesis and it depends on the corn price [S2, S0]. The corn price and the SPHP programme's volume, because they are the visible supports to that price — supports to monitor, not the mechanism through which the margin is being earned [S8, S9]. The working-capital ratio, because it is what separates the reported profit from the distributable cash and it is the reason our cash-flow value sits below the market [S0]. And the live-bird price, which we cannot source directly in this draft and which is the other half of the margin equation — a gap we intend to close at the first revision.

The monitoring list is deliberately short. In a commodity-input business the temptation is to track
everything; the discipline is to track the two or three variables that actually move the earnings,
and for an integrated poultry producer those are the feed grain price, the live-bird price and the
volume the institutional demand programmes deliver. Everything else — the segment mix, the
depreciation policy, the financing structure — changes slowly enough to be reviewed at results rather
than watched weekly.

bear.narrative: The margin gives the recovery back. Corn returns to the deck's forward curve, which sits well above the spot price CPIN paid in 2026 (S0), while broiler and DOC prices set daily in the market do not follow it up (S2, F3, F6); soymeal is imported and the rupiah is under balance-of-payments pressure (S0), so the protein input costs more in rupiah at the same dollar price. Demand also weakens: household purchasing power is already flagged as a drag on revenue in a source we cite for the sector (S6), and the recovery year is not repeated, so volume and price realisation fall together. The margin shock is widened to three points because it carries both the cost leg and a live-bird price fall, mirrored against the bull; no third unnamed haircut.

bull.narrative: The margin holds and the volume keeps coming. Corn stays near the spot level of 2026 rather than the deck's higher forward curve (S0), so the witnessed nine-month margin is held rather than given back; the free nutritious meals programme keeps adding institutional demand for chicken and eggs, which pulls through both the broiler and feed segments (S3); and the group's feed, DOC and processed-chicken chain lets it take that demand at its own margin rather than bidding for it. The two shocks mirror the bear exactly.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the nine-month actual, not on a forecast: nine-month 2026 net sales were IDR 60,200bn against IDR 50,600bn a year earlier, +19.0 per cent (S2, F1, F2). FY2025's fourth quarter contributed the difference between the audited year and its own nine-month base; running that quarter at the witnessed growth rate gives the FY2026E rate carried here. Growth then steps down to the volume the domestic market can absorb: the group has already taken the recovery year (nine-month segment sales of broiler IDR 26,980bn, feed IDR 20,740bn, processed chicken IDR 8,150bn, DOC IDR 3,440bn, S2, F3-F6) and no source discloses new capacity that would repeat a twenty per cent year. The taper is to the house macro deck's long-run expansion for Indonesia plus population, not a haircut (S0).

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The nine-month 2026 actual: net sales of IDR 60,200bn less cost of goods sold of IDR 49,600bn gives a gross margin near 17.6 per cent (S2, F1, F10), against 16.0 per cent in the same nine months of 2025 (IDR 50,600bn less IDR 42,500bn, S2, F2, F10) and 17.6 per cent for the whole of FY2025 (S0). The margin is at its own recent level, not stretched: cost of goods sold grew slower than sales while the corn price CPIN pays was below the deck's forward curve (S2, F10), and we hold the witnessed rate rather than extrapolate any further relief. The national SPHP feed-corn programme is a small, dated, reversible support for layer smallholders, not the reason a feed-to-plate group's margin is where it is: 242kt against a feed business selling IDR 20,740bn in nine months (S8, F31, S2, F4). The input is labelled "at base input costs" because the engine charges the deck's corn and soymeal curves through the two cost links after it (S0). The FY2026E value is set so that, after those links, the year whose first nine months are an actual is reproduced at the witnessed 17.6 per cent rather than overridden; it is a calibration to the reported nine months, and the realised margin it produces is published in section 3. From FY2027E the input is the witnessed rate itself and the deck's above-spot cost view bites, which is the 240bp give-back the base case carries.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 (corn): share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: An ordered estimate from the disclosed segments, because the company does not publish an input bill. Feed is IDR 20,740bn of IDR 60,200bn of nine-month sales, a third of the top line (S2, F4, F1); on a feed business that is mostly pass-through of raw material, feed is roughly a third of consolidated cost of goods sold. Corn is the industry's most important feed component (S8) and is conventionally rather more than half of a poultry feed formula, which puts corn at roughly one-fifth of group COGS. We carry that as an estimate and say so: the red team should read it as an ordered magnitude, not a disclosed number.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 (corn): pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Sixty per cent. Feed mills re-price bagged feed to farmers with a lag and broiler and DOC prices are set daily in a spot market the group does not clear, so a corn move reaches the P&L in part and over time rather than in full. The witnessed year supports a high pass-through rather than a squeeze: a 17 per cent rise in cost of goods sold on a 19 per cent rise in sales left the margin wider, not narrower (S2, F1, F2, F10).

assumptions.label: Cost link 2 (soymeal): share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: The same ordered estimate for the second input: soymeal is the protein component of the feed formula and, on the feed share of consolidated COGS set out in the corn line above (S2, F4), lands near one-tenth of group cost of goods sold. Soymeal is imported and priced in dollars, so this link also carries the rupiah. Disclosed as an estimate, not a sourced figure.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2 (soymeal): pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Sixty per cent, mirroring the corn link: the same feed-price lag and the same spot protein market sit behind both, and no source supports treating the two inputs differently. Mirroring keeps the two cost channels from smuggling an unstated margin assumption into the base case.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The last audited year's own selling and general expense over its own revenue, held flat in real terms across the forecast (S0). The engine's three-year default is higher because it averages in years with a weaker top line; the overhead base did not change with the recovery, so the ratio falls with sales rather than the cost being re-based.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(da, revenue))

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The last audited year's own capital spending over revenue, held flat (S0). That is the only witnessed ratio: the group bought breeding facilities from an affiliated company for IDR 430.98bn in August 2025 (S6, F30), an acquisition that sits in investing cash flow rather than in the capex line, and we do not gross it up into the forecast.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The declared ratio, not an assumption: the 2025 financial year was paid at a payout of 52.3 per cent of attributable profit (S5, F22), announced as 52.29 per cent with the IDR 180 per share distribution approved on 20 May 2026 (S7, F26, F27). The prior year was 47.7 per cent (S5), so the payout has stepped up rather than drifted, and we hold the current rate flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Set at 4.0 per cent, the rate every covered POULTRY_FEED peer (JPFA, MAIN, NEST, RLCO) uses on the same house macro deck, so the perpetuity is consistent across the industry rather than name-specific. It sits above the deck's 3.28 per cent CPI because it carries a little real volume: a protein business whose sales are nine-tenths domestic (S2, F8) grows with population and per-capita income, and its own revenue grew 4.8 per cent in a bad year (S5, F17). It remains below the deck's 5.29 per cent real GDP, so it does not assume share gain in perpetuity (S0).

challenges.challenge: The policy driver is over-read by an order of magnitude. S8 says Bapanas will distribute 242 thousand tonnes of feed corn in 2026 on a Rp678bn budget, up 372.6% on the 51.2kt actually delivered in 2025 to 3,578 layer farmers in 17 provinces, and the article's own scope is small and medium layer (egg) producers, with Bulog instructed not to ship subsidised corn into harvest-peak areas. The report uses it as "the input below the market price" for CPIN's whole cost base, "the reason the witnessed margin is where it is", the trigger of the bear scenario and driver two of the extreme_call justification. CPIN's feed segment alone sold Rp20,740bn in nine months; at any plausible corn price the national programme is a low-single-digit share of CPIN's corn, and the article names smallholders, not integrated producers, as recipients. A margin explanation that carries the thesis cannot rest on a programme this size and this target group.
challenges.answer: Demoted the SPHP programme: section 2 states 242kt is for layer smallholders and is not the margin mechanism; section 5 does not rely on it; scenario narratives and the extreme_call justification attribute the margin to the corn price running below the deck curve. S8 removed as driver two of extreme_call.

challenges.challenge: A key input the analyst knows is wrong was modelled around, not restated. D&A is Rp310bn against PPE of Rp18,060bn (1.7%) and capex of Rp1,771bn, and §3 says outright "the D&A line is the pack's and is likely understated". The MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE card says wrong data is restated, not modelled around. The damage runs in opposite directions on the two valuation legs: at a plausible 10% of PPE (Rp1,806bn) the P/E leg loses about Rp66 of EPS, i.e. about Rp970/share at 14.63x, while the DCF gains about Rp400bn a year of tax shield, i.e. roughly Rp250-300/share. So the error inflates the leg that gives the target its upside and deflates the leg that disciplines it, and the 217% divergence - the entire argument of §4 - is partly manufactured. §3's claim that understated D&A "flatters EBITDA" is also wrong: depreciation does not touch EBITDA.
challenges.answer: Partially. The false claim that understated D&A flatters EBITDA is removed and the gap is stated as an open data defect that understates the DCF tax shield and overstates EPS. The LK could not be reached from this environment, so da could not be restated as facts; this remains an open FATAL for the QC auditor, not a rebuttal.

challenges.challenge: The three methods do not share a horizon. P/E 5,035 is 14.63x FY2025A EPS of Rp344 and EV/EBITDA 5,058 is 10.36x FY2025A EBITDA of Rp8,443, while the DCF discounts FY2026E onward. Applied to FY2026E - the year the whole thesis is about - the same multiples give Rp6,188 and Rp6,154, a further +23% on the legs that already sit 217% above the primary. The report attributes the entire gap to "different questions", but part of it is simply a stale earnings base, and it matters because the blend is 50% of a DCF and 50% of two legs struck on a trough year.
challenges.answer: Each multiple leg is stated as FY2025A, with the reason and a note that FY2026E would be materially higher, so the published gap is a lower bound.

challenges.challenge: The mandatory multiple-survival test was not run. The DCF's terminal value of Rp32,701bn on FY2035E EBITDA of Rp9,541bn is a 3.43x exit EV/EBITDA, against 4.3x entry at the market price and a 10.36x cross-check multiple. A perpetuity that values the business at a third of the multiple the analyst says the market and peers pay is either a statement that the multiple is wrong or a statement that the DCF is; §4 never confronts it. This is the one test the method card calls mandatory, and it is the test that would have caught the reversed cross-check framing.
challenges.answer: Added the multiple-survival paragraph: terminal value share, implied exit multiple below the cross-check and the entry multiple, tension stated.

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF paragraph runs the wrong way. The DCF values the equity at Rp1,587, below the Rp2,370 price; to close that gap the implied perpetual growth must be HIGHER than 3.5% or the implied cost of capital LOWER than 11.9%. §4 says the price "implies a perpetual growth rate below the rate of inflation, or a cost of capital well above the house band", which is the arithmetic reversed, and it then builds the "market is pricing the cycle" conclusion on that inverted reading. The engine's own reverse_dcf returns available: false, "price not bracketed", so no computation backs the sentence.
challenges.answer: Reverse-DCF paragraph rewritten to the correct direction: DCF below price means a higher g or lower WACC is required, neither available.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 3.5% is the lowest in the industry and is a below-deck assumption. JPFA, MAIN, NEST and RLCO all run 4.0% on the same macro and agri decks; the deck carries Indonesia CPI at 3.28% and real GDP at 5.29%, so 3.5% is CPI plus 22bp of nominal growth, i.e. a perpetuity in which real volumes shrink, for a business whose sales are 99.6% domestic and whose own revenue grew 4.8% in a bad year. The justification given ("CPI rather than nominal GDP") is a policy preference, not a source, and the terminal value is 38.3% of DCF EV and about 19% of the target. Compounding it with C3's trough-year multiples, the base case is conservative in at least two independent places at once, which the card warns is as wrong as the opposite.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth moved to 4.0 per cent, the rate every covered POULTRY_FEED peer uses on the same deck, with the real-volume reason.

challenges.challenge: The leverage the prose describes is not the leverage the model deducts. §3 says "Net debt was IDR2,201bn at the last audited year-end, or 0.3 times EBITDA" and calls the balance sheet unlevered; the valuation deducts Rp4,480.7bn, which is the 30 June 2026 pack balance sheet (cash 5,368, debt 9,849), and the same June balance sheet shows net working capital up from Rp16,106bn to Rp18,944bn, +17.6% against nine-month revenue running +13.5% annualised. The working-capital build the report names as its main DCF drag is already happening faster than sales, and the reader is told about a balance sheet six months and Rp2.3trn out of date. Net debt/EBITDA on the June figure is 0.5x on FY2025A EBITDA, not 0.3x.
challenges.answer: Section 3 states that the valuation deducts the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, net debt more than double the FY2025A figure and about half a turn, and that working capital already rose faster than sales; the build is in the bear case.

challenges.challenge: S6 is cited only for the Rp430.98bn breeding acquisition, but its opening paragraph says CPIN's revenue this year "diproyeksi konservatif bahkan lebih rendah akibat pelemahan daya beli masyarakat" - projected weaker on softening household purchasing power. That is a demand-side downside in a source the report already trusts, and it is nowhere in §5, which lists policy reversal, free-meal reshuffling, FX and disease but not consumer demand. Combined with the bear's design (growth -3pp, margin -2pp, no price shock at all), the bear never tests a live-bird or DOC price fall, which the report itself says is half of the margin equation and which the peer set [S3: SIPD swung to a Rp59bn loss, WMUU still loss-making on +62.8% revenue] shows is real.
challenges.answer: Added the purchasing-power downside (S6) and a price-realisation shock: bear margin shock widened to three points, mirrored in the bull.

challenges.challenge: The forward earnings and yield argument - the strongest bull case in the file - is never stated. Nine-month EPS is Rp316 [S2, F13], so the run-rate is about Rp421 and the shares at Rp2,370 are on 5.6x; on the model's own FY2026E dividend of Rp221 the forward yield is 9.3%, against a 7.6% trailing yield and a payout the board has just raised to 52.3%. The report quotes 6.9x trailing and the historical 52.3% payout but never the run-rate multiple or the forward yield, and the bull scenario (+3pp growth, +2pp margin) does not restore the witnessed margin: FY2027E gross margin is 15.25% realised against 17.63% witnessed, so even the bull sits below what the company has actually just earned.
challenges.answer: Investment summary carries the nine-month EPS run-rate, the single-digit forward multiple and the forward dividend yield.

challenges.challenge: The free nutritious meals programme is described as a volume driver [S3] and then given no value anywhere in the model: revenue growth tapers 19% -> 7% -> 4.5% with no institutional-demand leg, and the bull shocks only growth and margin by 3pp/2pp. S3 is explicit that kitchens scaling up pull through DOC and feed demand, which are the two segments where the integration argument is strongest (DOC Rp3.44trn and feed Rp20.74trn of nine-month sales, [S2]). If the programme is a named catalyst in §7 and a named bear risk in §5, it should also be a named bull driver with a number.
challenges.answer: Section 2 states the programme cannot be quantified from the sources held, carries no volume in base or bull, and is a signpost not a valued catalyst.

challenges.challenge: Two shareholding registers are asserted to be consistent and are not. S5 gives the group 55.53%, public investors 38.49% and UBS AG Singapore 5.98%; the pack gives free float 15.41% and insiders 71.51% [S0, IDX-IC mirror]. Public 38.49% and free float 15.41% cannot both be right, and 55.53 + 5.98 = 61.5% does not equal 71.51% either. §6 calls them "consistent with that structure" and §1 calls 15.4% "a thin float for a company of this size", which is the basis for accepting a 0% liquidity discount. On the pack's numbers the free float is Rp6.0trn against Rp96.2bn of daily turnover, i.e. 1.6% of float a day - not thin at all; on S5's numbers it is Rp15.0trn and 0.6%.
challenges.answer: Registers no longer called consistent: gap disclosed, pack float used for the liquidity test, turnover as a share of float stated, zero discount justified.

challenges.challenge: The gross-margin input is a plug and the report only ever shows the input, never the realised path. FY2026E gross_margin is set at 19.95% - 235bp above the disclosed 17.63% and above the FY2025A actual of 17.57% - with the stated purpose of cancelling the deck's above-spot corn and soymeal through the cost links, so realised FY2026E comes out at 17.66% and the calibration gate passes by construction. From FY2027E the input is 17.6% and the links take realised margin to 15.25%, a 240bp compression below the last actual that drives the -14% EBITDA step in FY2027E (Rp10,173bn -> Rp8,709bn). The report's model table shows the EBITDA drop but not the margin that causes it, and a reader cannot tell that the base case assumes a 240bp margin give-back.
challenges.answer: Section 3 publishes the realised gross-margin path and explains the give-back as the deck curves above the spot price CPIN paid.

challenges.challenge: The governance section rates the name while listing the checks it did not run. It admits "we have not been able to source a full related-party flow table" and "we have not been able to source the audit opinion or the auditor identity", yet concludes that control is "neither a red flag nor a protection" and that the acquisition is "an internal reorganisation rather than a value transfer". EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS makes related-party flow quantification and auditor/notation status a pre-thesis gate on IDX, and this group buys feed inputs from CP affiliates at scale - exactly the modal channel the card names. No accruals ratio, no pledge check, no board-notation check is recorded either, although accruals are computable from the pack (FY2025 (5,644 - 5,774)/44,325 = -0.3%, i.e. clean, which the report should say).
challenges.answer: Governance conclusion downgraded to not assessed; accruals clean; pledge/notation/auditor recorded as unassessed gaps.

challenges.challenge: Two unit errors and one band error. §5 gives three-month average daily turnover as "IDR96,173,548,323bn", which is Rp96.2 quintillion; the pack figure is Rp96.17bn. §3 says operating profit "recovered to 8,133.1" with no unit (IDR bn). §4 says COE of 13.04% "sits inside the house band" of 11-13%; it is 4bp outside it, so the sentence "no argument is needed" is not quite true.
challenges.answer: Turnover renders as IDR96.2bn, operating profit carries IDRbn, COE sentence corrected to top of house band.

challenges.challenge: The published sensitivity table is transposed. sensitivities[0] declares x = WACC and y = terminal growth, but the array is indexed [growth][WACC]: the centre row varies with growth (1,789 at g-1pp to 1,427 at g+1pp, i.e. value FALLING as growth rises) and the centre column varies with WACC (1,505 at WACC-1pp to 1,691 at WACC+1pp, value RISING with discount rate). Recomputed directly from the FCFF rows, the correct direction is +50bp of g = about +Rp50 and -50bp of WACC = about +Rp50. A reader who takes the printed axes at face value reads the sign backwards on both.
challenges.answer: The grid is indexed [growth][WACC] and its directions are correct: within a row value falls as WACC rises, down a column value rises with growth; the review read rows as the x axis. Added the convention to the report.

missing_bull_case.note: The strongest bull argument in the file is never written down: nine-month EPS of Rp316 [S2, F13] annualises to about Rp421, so the shares are on 5.6x run-rate earnings and a 9.3% FY2026E dividend yield on a 52.3% payout, which is an income floor the price is ignoring. The free-meals programme's DOC and feed pull-through [S3] is described in §2 and then given no volume in the model, not even in the bull. C9, C10.

missing_bear_case.note: The text says net debt is IDR2,201bn and 0.3x EBITDA (Dec-2025) while the valuation deducts IDR4,480.7bn (Jun-2026) - the leverage the model uses is more than twice the leverage the prose describes, and working capital already rose 17.6% in six months against 13.5% annualised revenue. S6, cited for the acquisition, opens by flagging weakening household purchasing power as a drag on revenue, and §5's bear never shocks price (only volume and margin). C7, C8.

assumption_realism.note: D&A runs at 1.7% of PPE (Rp310bn on Rp18,060bn) and the analyst says so but leaves the engine default in place, against the method card's rule that wrong data is restated. The FY2026E gross margin input of 19.95% sits 235bp above the disclosed 17.6% and exists only to cancel the deck's cost links; realised FY2026E is 17.66% and realised FY2027E is 15.25%, a 240bp base-case compression the report never shows. The corn/soymeal shares (19%/9%) are declared estimates, which is honest, but they are the inputs the margin depends on. C2, C12.

evidence_and_citations.note: S8 is 242kt and Rp678bn for 2026, aimed at small and medium layer farmers, and the report turns it into "the input below the market price" for a feed-to-plate group and "the single thing an investor is underwriting" - the quote does not support the claim. Free float 15.41%/insider 71.51% [S0] is called "consistent with" S5's 38.49% public/55.53% group/5.98% UBS, a 23pp and 10pp gap. The related-party flow table is admitted unsourced and no pledge, board-notation or audit-opinion check is recorded. C1, C11, C13.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary is right for the industry and the COE build (7.4%/4.2%/2.5%, beta 1.08, 13.04%/11.89%) is shown and in band. But P/E 5,035 and EV/EBITDA 5,058 are struck on FY2025A EPS 344 and EBITDA 8,443 while the DCF discounts from FY2026E; on FY2026E the same multiples give 6,188 and 6,154, so the 217% divergence the report explains at length is partly a horizon artifact. The mandatory multiple-survival test is absent: the terminal value implies 3.43x exit EV/EBITDA. C3, C4, C5.

bias_and_tone.note: To its credit §4 says plainly that the DCF is below the price and that a cash-flow reader should not own it, which is more candour than this desk usually gets. But calling a method that says -33% "primary" while giving it 50% and then buying on the other 50% is a conclusion the evidence does not carry, and the reverse-DCF sentence runs the wrong way. The bear at Rp3,065 is above the price, so the published bear still says buy. C5, C7.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Corn and soymeal are read off d.agri and the rev/gross-margin path is consistent with JPFA's structure; terminal growth is not. CPIN uses g = 3.5% while JPFA, MAIN, NEST and RLCO all use 4.0% on the same deck, with no name-specific reason. The imported soymeal link is not wired to usd_idr (deck 18,350 vs spot 18,049), so the FX channel the bear narrative relies on does not actually reach the model. C6.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked conservatism on the value drivers: terminal g 3.5% (lowest in the industry, = deck CPI with zero real growth, no source, 38% of DCF EV); multiple legs applied to the FY2025A trough year (-Rp1,100/share on each leg); D&A at 1.7% of PPE suppressing the DCF through an inflated tax bill. Against these, the one optimism is the FY2026E margin plug. The stack moves the target by well over 10% in either direction, which is why C2, C3 and C6 are challenges rather than notes.

calibration.note: fund record qc passes clean: one BLOCK flag (extreme_call) and no errors, FY2025A EBITDA margin actual 11.94% vs model 12.09%, gap 0.15pp; FY2026E lands at 12.09% against 11.94% last actual, so the base does reproduce the last year. The gate is in-sample, though, and cannot see the 235bp gross-margin plug that makes it pass; and the extreme_call justification names S8 as driver two, which S8 does not support. C1, C12.

signoff.notes: Approved. Round-1 FATAL C1 (SPHP programme over-read) is fixed on substance and the programme is demoted in §2/§5. C2's D&A line is a disclosed data defect, not an assumption: the report states its direction and the P/E leg is the one affected, and the call survives the correction (the P/E leg loses about Rp290/share at 30% weight; the DCF tax shield moves the other way). Every MATERIAL is answered or disclosed, QC PASS and lint PASS. The BUY rests on the disclosed 50/30/20 blend: the DCF alone says Rp1,636 against a Rp2,370 price and the report says so plainly. Carry the D&A restatement and the forward-year multiple sensitivity into the next refresh; they do not block this initiation.

bias.note: Round-1 BLOCK Q1 is fixed at the filter and verified in the render: the forward dividend yield prints 9.3% (221/2,370, matching mult.FY2026E.div_yield 0.0933) and both market-value instances (sections 1 and 5) print IDR38,863.3bn from mkt.mcap_idr of 38,863,260,000,000, i.e. IDR38.86trn; a full sweep of the rendered report finds no tn/quintillion figure and no unresolved template field. Q2 is fixed in the right direction: section 3 now says depreciation does not touch EBITDA, that the multiple legs are struck on reported FY2025A EPS and EBITDA which a forecast da_pct never enters, and that the one measurable effect - forecast depreciation of 0.49% of revenue against capex of 2.5% - understates the DCF tax shield, so the DCF is too low rather than too high, with the target not raised on the multiple legs while the line is unsourced. Q3 is fixed: section 4 states the implied re-rating (14.63x against the 6.9x trailing multiple), names the two populations averaged, and says peer-anchored the target would not exist.
